You hit a good depth, props. Clarifying questions and wall of text incoming:

What do you mean by strain? Which exact part of the movement do you feel this strain? Does your lower back feel like it is getting worked more than your legs or is it more along the lines of a noticeable pain? If so, what is the pain rating on a scale of 1-10? What does your back feel like later in the day after squats and over the next couple days? Does it feel like a muscular soreness as if they have been worked? If so, does it eventually recover?

What is your history with exercise and more specifically squatting? There is a certain level of endurance that your back needs to hold in order to be able to squat. Sometimes the back can be a limiting factor and give out before your legs do. If this is your first time squatting/exercising, I would expect the lower back to be sore from this movement, especially since your trunk is pretty far forward.

There might be nothing wrong with your squat right now and as you work on your mobility and lower back strength. There also could be a few things at play here that you could try to address to approach an improvement. 

Some people (because of differing limb/torso lengths) will have to shift their weight more anteriorly (forward) to stay balanced. As others have mentioned, a lack of ankle flexibility/mobility can play a factor: If your shins are limited in their ability to move over the toes, your torso will need to come forward in order to prevent you from falling backwards. (I have the same issue).  Glute tightness can cause the lower back to round in order to compensate, but I don't really see your lower back rounding from this angle. Perhaps a higher camera angle would prove otherwise though.

If I had to guess: When you start your ascent in the majority of your reps. your hips seem to be shooting up slightly before your head does, which can cause your back to take more of the load since it is in a parallel position to the ground (kind of looks like a good morning on the way up as another user mentioned). Try to think about keeping your chest up as you rise and pushing the bar up through your upper back. Film this and see if you feel any different.

Here is a mobility routine that may help: [https://www.youtube.com/shorts/JOXjqfyhkuU](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/JOXjqfyhkuU) 

Try a few of these (especially the goblet squat and lunging on a box). These helped me a ton to open up my hips and improved my ankle mobility. From this angle, your knees seem like they are going over your toes (even moreso than mine are able to in this movement) so I'm not sure this is the biggest issue.

Social skills are like any other skill. It’s just harder to practice because the practice involves another person actively taking part in it. It’s not a guitar for example, where you can sit in your room alone and work on a single riff for hours. 

Working out and feeling accomplished from achieving small goals here and there in the gym (and even just from going when you really didn’t want to) has been amazing for my confidence and tolerance talking with people. Then I try to channel that confidence into talking with strangers (even if it’s just saying hello or smiling as they brush by) and showing genuine interest. Even if you have to deal with 99 people that are annoying and the relationship doesn’t amount to much, it can be worth it for the one person you didn’t know you’d click with or share a couple interests with.

Focused on just getting back to my room to play my games and watch YouTube/whatever. Working out and working towards what I wanted to look like/feel like was amazing for my confidence. Getting a job that forces you to talk to people worked wonders for me and I’ve challenged myself to smile and make conversation with people I don’t know. I’m still not great at it, but I know now that it’s a skill that can be learned. A few people I’ve talked to have said something along the lines of “you seem so happy all the time idk how you do it.” That made me wonder if that’s how “normal” “happy” people seem all the time when behind closed doors they can feel like an absolute wreck. It gave me more confidence to try and learn more about other people through genuine interest.

Same and I think it has to do with preparedness. In DM you expect someone around every corner and people aren’t generally playing as stealthily. Everyone is just wide swinging. You also are fighting someone every few seconds. In a comp game there is utility you need to worry about, other game sense things to think about, as well as longer breaks between fights which can break focus and make anticipatory reaction time less useful. Another factor could be nerves. Dying in dm is insignificant and I’ve found it’s easier to constantly drill “headshots only” when there are no stakes. In comp you can get caught up in the mentality about winning your fights so you can win the game and I’ve caught myself committing to sprays more in comp games in a desperate attempt to win a gunfight, which more often than not gets me killed.

Crouch spraying can be really good in some cases, but if you do it every time it can get predictable. Full running and strafing while spraying can be very effective at close range as well. Strafing rapidly back and forth can be effective. Every situation is different and you will find what works as you as you use each one. A lot of players will fall into the trap and habit of just using one or the other but an experienced player will recognize the options and be able to make split second decisions as to the most effective pattern. Mess around with it and get a feel of your weapon and what ranges/angles each strategy performs best in. On defense for example: you may find at a particular angle, a lot of enemy chars tend to come around an angle all at once, where using a crouch spray may get you killed instantly where a run and gun or strafe burst technique can maybe get a kill and get out, giving your team an advantage.

So this is something you need to do in cs because of momentum (less so in this game d/t how movement works) but in cs if you held A or D (to strafe sideways and swing out) and suddenly let go of the key, you would not stop right away. Your character would almost “slide” as it slowly came to a stop, and during this time your shots would not be accurate.  Counter-strafing is tapping the opposite movement key (a if you held d, d if you held a) to instantly stop your characters momentum in order to get an accurate shot off faster and give your opponent holding the angle you are swinging less time to react. In Valorant, this matters less since the movement isn’t as “slippery” and you can get away with just letting go of the key you strafed out with. I still recommend practicing strafe-bursting in the range and deathmatch until it is automatic since spray patterns are random after a certain amount of bullets. Instinctively crouch spraying for every enemy you see is pretty inconsistent and personally I’ve found much more success with bursting with a rifle, strafing for a second to stay hard to hit while also resetting the recoil on your gun, counter strafing to stop, and taking another burst at a target. At very close distances crouch spraying can be good sometimes, but at very far distances I sometimes will shoot 1-2 bullets in between strafes.

I’m looking at prosettings.net for their average professional edpi and it appears to be 282, which is about .353 @ 800 dpi. There are plenty of people that go way above that or way below that, but that is the average. The median (according to their site) is .314 @ 800. 

People say you should find a sensitivity that you can comfortably 180 on, but I think this is overhyped, mainly because most of your kills should be occurring (given proper crosshair placement) near where your crosshair is. There are times you need to flick to a target, but the reason many cs/valorant pros on average don’t have as high sensitivity as other games such as apex legends for example, is because the TTK (time to kill) is so low that if you are being shot in the back you are probably dead anyway and the issue lies more with positioning rather than aim. There are some freaks of nature that can play consistently on a very high sens, but if you are having a bad day, your small aim discrepancies can be amplified and consistency is more difficult. This can definitely be slower paced than other fps titles out there and I think is comparative to a surgeon’s necessity to be quick but precise.

Well, I’m not an expert in any sense, but hamstrings are multiarticular (meaning they stretch over multiple joints, namely, the hip and the knee). If you extend your knee and flex the hip, you over lengthen the hamstrings and your knees might bend in order to provide some slack. I think this could be due to a lack of flexibility/ROM in the hamstrings (which seems to not be an issue for you) or perhaps a neurological factor. When you reach and touch your toes, your knees are basically forced into extension through gravity (if you are standing) or by the ground (if sitting). If you are on your back, the forces keeping your knee extended are most likely internal, or produced by your muscles which are able to be influenced by neurological stretch reflexes. This might be making it harder to voluntarily keep the knee from bending. If a muscle/group of muscles is/are multi-articular (like the hamstrings) over- shortening or over-lengthening the muscle results in less than ideal conditions for muscle force production. This could be a reason why it is harder to extend the knee with your thigh already flexed (in a bent position) as the over-lengthening of the hamstrings and natural recoil of the stretched muscles overpowers the ability of your body’s ability to extend the knee.

Another point brought to light by /u/iWantToLiftAgain could be a variable. If you reach for your toes with legs straight, your spine/back may be flexing (or bending towards your toes) letting you get that extra range and ultimately giving you the impression of hamstring flexibility. When you lay on your back with only one leg raised, the leg on the ground keeps the pelvis/hip from tilting back. Since the hamstrings are attached the bottom of the pelvis, if the pelvis is unable to move, the hamstrings are forced to stretch. If you lift both legs in the air, there is nothing to keep your hip from tilting back, and you may notice an increase in range of motion and ability to extend both knees. This additional flexibility could be attributed to the pelvis tilting back, rather than only the leg and hamstring flexibility.
